Fredrik Gustafsson / Linköping

Find the signal in the noise

Fredrik Gustafsson is a signal professor in the broadest sense: someone who looks for meaningful structure in noisy reality. He likes problems that matter, people he enjoys, challenges that are difficult as hell, and ideas exciting enough to steal time from golf.

He moves between mathematics and field reality with little respect for disciplinary borders, turning uncertain measurements into decisions, research into systems, and occasionally equations into companies.

Nature, competition, family, humour and a portable espresso machine belong to the same story.

Having achieved most of the conventional things he once aimed for, he is now in the fortunate and slightly dangerous position of being free to see what turns up next.

Professor · Researcher · Entrepreneur · Occasionally found in trees

Academic

Signalprofessor has many publications, many citations and a reassuringly large h-index. Google Scholar keeps count.

I'm more interested in the research ideas that survived long enough to become useful.

Four of them have followed me for much of my career: detecting change, extracting information from moving vehicles, representing uncertainty, and figuring out where things are.

Things that change

My PhD thesis in 1992 was about change detection: how to notice quickly that the system producing your measurements isn't the system you thought it was.

The technical thread connects system identification, filtering, statistical inference, and discrete decisions: estimate what can be estimated, then decide whether the system producing the measurements has changed.

The thesis eventually became Adaptive Filtering and Change Detection (Wiley, 2000)—essentially my PhD thesis 2.0.

Change detection has kept coming back in different disguises. Twenty years later, work with Henrik Ohlsson, Lennart Ljung and Stephen Boyd revisited the problem through sparse estimation. That paper received the 2012 Automatica Best Paper Award.

More recently it turned up again in monitoring failures in implanted HeartMate pumps.

Apparently some research problems are difficult to get rid of.

Selected work → Thesis · Book · Automatica Best Paper · HeartMate monitoring

Cars, tyres and roads

My first serious application area was cars.

Can a car infer what is happening between tyre and road from sensors it already has?

Tyre–road friction is difficult to measure directly. It changes with the road, weather, tyres and vehicle dynamics, and becomes most important precisely when safety margins are small.

The work became an early exercise in virtual sensing: use models and signals already available in the vehicle to estimate a quantity that would otherwise require another physical sensor.

That question led to MSc projects, patents and research on tyre–road friction estimation, including an Automatica paper in 1997.

A few years later, some of the equations escaped.

→ NIRA Dynamics, 2001

A cloud of particles

In the late 1990s, Arnaud Doucet and Christophe Andrieu visited Linköping and introduced us to a beautifully simple idea.

Instead of forcing a complicated probability distribution into a convenient Gaussian shape, represent it by a cloud of samples.

Particle filters were exactly the kind of method we liked: elegant theory, computationally demanding, and immediately useful for difficult nonlinear problems.

Niclas Bergman was working on terrain-aided navigation for Gripen and promptly gave particle filters something unusually convincing to do.

Research that flies. For real.

In 2002 we tried to summarize what we had learned in Particle Filters for Positioning, Navigation, and Tracking.

Particle filters then spread through the research group into positioning, tracking, navigation and sensor fusion across generations of PhD students.

Twenty-four years later, IEEE decided the paper had survived rather well: it received the IEEE Signal Processing Society Sustained Impact Paper Award.

Selected work → 2002 paper · Particle-filter theory and practice

Where am I?

Around the same time, Fredrik Gunnarsson and I started asking a more general question:

What can radio signals actually tell us about position—and how accurately can we possibly know?

Our 2005 paper put heterogeneous radio measurements, geometry, maps, motion models and other sensors into one statistical estimation framework.

A central part was not only estimating position, but understanding fundamental accuracy limits: how measurement quality and geometry constrain the performance any method can achieve.

The measurements changed. Mobile networks went from GSM through 3G, 4G and 5G. Now 6G is beginning. Smartphones added inertial sensors and richer maps, but the same framework—measurements, geometry, motion, uncertainty and fusion—remains relevant.

The underlying questions changed remarkably little.

And some of those equations eventually escaped indoors.

→ Senion, 2010

And then there are the side quests

The four threads above explain much of my research career. Fortunately, not all of it.

And then there was a pandemic.

Suddenly estimating hidden states from noisy measurements was everybody's problem.

Together with researchers in control, statistics, epidemiology and healthcare, we worked on intervention effects, infection rates, hospitalisation forecasts and uncertainty.

One result ended up in Nature.

The journal, not the place where you find rhinos.

Show me the equations →

Sometimes people ask us to locate things.

A ferry in the Baltic Sea without using GPS.

A missing aircraft in the Indian Ocean.

Different sensors. Different stakes. Same irritating question:

Where are you?

Occasionally, the equations escape the university

I like research that produces papers. I like it even more when the results acquire a life outside the university.

A company is one way an idea can learn to move without its originator.

Looking back, the companies aren't quite as random as they seem.

1998 — Sigmoid

I like new ideas.

My first company, and still my playground for new projects.

SIGnals, MOdels and IDentification.

It also refers to the sigmoid function in neural networks.

And if someone asks rudely enough, I explain that sigmoid is Latin for asshole. Close enough.

2001 — NIRA Dynamics

I like cars.

Remember the tyre–road friction research?

Some of those equations escaped.

NIRA Dynamics grew from vehicle models that used existing signals to estimate quantities otherwise requiring additional physical sensors.

Today its indirect tyre-pressure monitoring technology is found in around 140 million cars.

The same virtual-sensing philosophy has moved from understanding the car to understanding the road. Last winter, NIRA delivered around 300 million road-friction measurements to Trafikverket.

Show me the equations →

2003 — Softube

I like rock'n'roll.

Then the equations found a guitar amplifier.

System identification means building models of dynamic systems from measured inputs and outputs. Here, the systems were analogue audio equipment and the outputs had to sound right.

Softube grew from that collision of engineering and music.

Today the brand is used by countless professional producers, GRAMMY-winning engineers and artists worldwide.

Same equations. More distortion.

Show me the equations →

2010 — Senion

I don't like shopping malls.

The original problem was positioning firefighters and first responders inside buildings, where GPS is unavailable.

Senion combined smartphone radio measurements, inertial sensors, maps and Bayesian sensor fusion to estimate position indoors.

The technology eventually found itself in large shopping centres around the world and later in smart offices.

Senion was acquired by Verizon in 2021.

So apparently I helped create a company that made it easier to find my way out of shopping malls.

Show me the equations →

2021 — Qulinda

I like animals and nature.

Eventually, the signals grew legs.

Qulinda brings positioning, sensors, communications and AI to livestock in Sweden and wildlife in Africa.

The questions are concrete:

Where is the animal? What is it doing? Is something unusual happening? Does someone need to know?

Into the wild

In January 2014, Johan Bergenäs took me to Ngulia Rhino Sanctuary in Kenya.

I had been interested in nature since I was a boy. But this was different.

There were endangered rhinos worth protecting, poachers trying to kill them, and rangers expected to patrol an enormous protected area with limited resources and difficult conditions.

As an engineer, it was difficult not to start thinking.

The first useful thing we built wasn't a sensor.

It was an app.

WildProtect digitised patrol and wildlife observations so rangers and commanders could build shared situational awareness. Rangers needed better information before they needed better gadgets.

The gadgets came later.

Phones → tracking tags → cameras → drones → radar → microphones → geophones → AI → BLE scanners in acacia trees

Wildlife Security grew into a research programme combining positioning, camera traps, tracking tags, radar, acoustic and seismic sensing, communications, AI and decision support.

What started as a security project gradually became a place where engineers, biologists, students, rangers and conservationists could work on the same problems from completely different directions.

Students started coming with us to Africa. Their MSc projects stopped being PDFs and became systems they had to install, explain, debug and leave working.

Power fails. Networks disappear. Animals don't read specifications. Users have opinions.

Heat, dust, scarce power, unreliable connectivity, limited ground truth, false alarms and maintenance are part of the system—not inconveniences outside it.

Excellent research environment.

The direction is now broader: animal behaviour, livestock, conservation, coexistence and environmental monitoring. Qulinda and Smart Savannahs connect that work to practical systems and long-term conservation efforts without changing the central question: what is happening, where, and does someone need to know?

More than ten years later, I'm still climbing trees.

Out of office

I grew up in Aneby.

Before there were wildlife sensors, there was a boy looking for birds and playing football.

Chess took over when I was thirteen. Running came at university. Golf arrived eventually.

Four children arrived over a rather longer interval.

And espresso appears to have become infrastructure.

The first Starbucks in Spain was opening the next morning. I found it the night before, tried the locked door and looked sufficiently disappointed that the CEO let me in.

He and the chairman had flown in from Seattle for the opening.

So we had an espresso.

Why Signalprofessor?

Apparently I am signalprofessor at Gmail, Chess.com, Lichess, Strava, Garmin Golf and Nespresso, among other places.

At this point it seemed easier to buy the domain.

So why all these things?

Change detection. Cars. Particle filters. Radio positioning. Companies. Pandemics. Rhinos. Chess. Drones. Heartbeats.

Seen as a list, my career is not particularly coherent.

It feels more coherent from the inside.

There are far more interesting problems than I could possibly work on, so over the years I seem to have developed a filter.

The S4 rule. Four S's—fyra ess i leken.

Still looking for signal.

I don't know what the next project will be. That's rather the point.

I am particularly interested in problems where statistical inference, sensing and real-world systems meet—and where solving the technical problem would actually make something better.

If it has societal value, involves good people, is difficult as hell and makes me genuinely curious, it has passed the first test.
